title: Gurmat sangeet
hook: schools teaching the ragas of the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, katha traditions, the many ways Gurbani is opened up aloud. Your line was many ways to explain.

A classroom with no desks. Students sit cross-legged on a rug, each with a long-necked string instrument resting against one shoulder, a bow in the other hand. The teacher sings a short phrase. The students play it back, a little ragged. The teacher sings it again, slower, bending one note just so. They try again. Down the hall, someone is practicing the same phrase alone, over and over. Nobody here is rehearsing for a concert. They're learning to sing scripture in the ragas its own headings name. Today's word is the name for that music.
screen: `A ROOM WITH NO DESKS.` → `THE TEACHER SINGS; THEY PLAY IT BACK.` → `SCRIPTURE, AS ITS HEADINGS ASK.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Gurmat means the Guru's way, the Guru's teaching; sangeet means music. Gurmat sangeet is the music of the Guru's way: kirtan sung in the ragas the Guru Granth Sahib names, with the care the book itself asks for. Second, why it needs schools. A raga isn't something you pick up from one hearing. Each has its own notes, its own climbing and falling, its own feeling, learned slowly at a teacher's feet. So schools and teachers keep raga kirtan alive, and pass it on student by student. Third, the instruments. Alongside the harmonium heard in gurdwaras today, these schools often teach the older string instruments: the rabab, the saranda, the taus, the dilruba. Some teachers say the strings can follow the bends of a raga's notes more closely. Others play the harmonium with great skill. Both are heard. Fourth, what the ragas carry. A raga has a mood, and Gurbani knows it. In a var in Raag Malar, the monsoon raga, Guru Amar Das says, in paraphrase: Malar is a cooling raga, and meditating on the Lord brings peace. Notice where the peace comes from: the raga sets the mood, and the remembering does the rest. That's what these schools keep: not music for its own sake, but a sound shaped to help the words land. When a student sings the Malar hymns in Malar, the music and the scripture speak together, under the heading the book gives them.
screen: `GURMAT: THE GURU'S WAY. SANGEET: MUSIC.` · `A RAGA TAKES YEARS TO LEARN.` · `RABAB, SARANDA, TAUS, DILRUBA.` · `MALAR IS A COOLING RAGA.` · then, large: `KEEPING THE RAGAS.`

segments.voice: Today's raga is Malar, the monsoon raga, the cooling one; say its name once, softly. Then pair it with a sound you already know, rain on a roof after a hot day, and say the name again on the out-breath, slowly, letting the rain sit behind it.
Gurmat sangeet. The music of the Guru's way: kirtan sung in the ragas the Guru Granth Sahib names, kept alive by schools and teachers. Today's word.
Your line: keeping the ragas. Slow learning, passed from teacher to student. See you on the path tomorrow.

chat.says: Why would Sikhs need whole schools just to sing hymns?
options: Because each raga has its own notes, movement and mood, and learning one takes slow work with a teacher.
Because the hymns are secret, and only school graduates may sing them in a gurdwara.
Because the hymns change every year, and schools teach everyone the newest version.
